title: Applied and Agentic AI Production Curriculum Expansion
authority: These records add approved curriculum depth. Third-party program descriptions are comparison sources, not water-sector authority or permission to reproduce course content. Every factual learner claim remains subject to source, practitioner, technical, accessibility, and release review.

sources.title: Applied AI Bundle: Generative and Agentic AI
Certificate Program in AI and Agentic AI Engineering

expansions.title: The production AI lifecycle, from evidence to operation
expansions.description: Connect data, model or language-system design, evaluation, release, monitoring, incident response, rollback, and improvement in one traceable lifecycle. The learner should see that a working demonstration is only one controlled stage.
objectives: Explain the difference among experiment, demonstration, pilot, production service, and governed operating capability.
Trace one utility application through data, model, prompt, context, tool, evaluation, release, monitoring, incident, rollback, and correction records.
Identify the owner, evidence, entry condition, exit condition, and stop rule at every lifecycle gate.
Distinguish a model change from a data, retrieval, prompt, tool, permission, interface, or workflow change.
Create and defend a production AI lifecycle and provenance card for a bounded utility use case.
subtopics: Experiment, demonstration, pilot, production, and retirement
Data, model, prompt, context, tool, and configuration versions
Evaluation and acceptance before release
Environment promotion and accountable approval
Monitoring, incident, correction, rollback, and retirement
One traceable record from source evidence to operating decision
expansions.workProduct: production AI lifecycle and provenance card
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Do not treat a stage name, vendor platform, deployment, or passing test as proof that a utility application is safe, useful, supported, or approved.

expansions.title: Machine Learning Operations pipelines and reproducibility
expansions.description: Teach the operating pipeline that moves data, code, model artifacts, tests, approvals, and monitoring through controlled environments. The learner must be able to reproduce a release and recover from a failed one.
objectives: Explain Machine Learning Operations in plain English as the controlled path from model work to supported operation.
Map data, code, experiment, model, test, environment, release, monitoring, and rollback dependencies.
Distinguish version control, experiment tracking, artifact storage, continuous integration, continuous delivery, and deployment.
Diagnose a reproducibility failure and identify the missing version, dependency, data, or configuration evidence.
Create a vendor-neutral Machine Learning Operations pipeline and release record.
subtopics: Pipeline architecture and responsibility
Data, code, model, configuration, and environment versions
Experiment tracking and artifact lineage
Automated tests and continuous integration
Release approval, deployment strategies, and rollback
Performance degradation, data drift, model drift, and correction
expansions.workProduct: Machine Learning Operations pipeline and release record
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Use synthetic or approved data. Do not represent a classroom pipeline as a supported production service or a validated predictive model.

expansions.title: Large Language Model Operations and agent operations
expansions.description: Unify prompt, context, retrieval, tools, models, evaluations, traces, cost, incidents, and human review as one operating discipline for language-model and agent systems.
objectives: Explain how Large Language Model Operations differs from ordinary model deployment and ordinary software operation.
Version prompts, system instructions, retrieval sources, tools, permissions, evaluations, and model choices as operating dependencies.
Inspect a trace and separate model, source, tool, permission, orchestration, and human-review failures.
Define operating measures for quality, groundedness, refusal, tool correctness, latency, cost, and review effort.
Create an agent operations record with monitoring, incident, rollback, and human-escalation rules.
subtopics: Prompt, context, retrieval, model, tool, and policy versions
Offline evaluation, regression testing, and online observation
Traces, tool calls, state transitions, and human review
Latency, token use, cost limits, rate limits, and capacity
Agent incidents, containment, retry limits, escalation, and rollback
Ownership, service levels, support, and retirement
expansions.evidenceBoundary: A trace shows what the system recorded. It does not prove completeness, correctness, legal sufficiency, or professional judgment.

expansions.title: Agents, goals, environments, and perceived agency
expansions.description: Give learners a precise model for what an agent observes, what it may do, what goal it is pursuing, what environment it operates in, and why people can perceive more intelligence or authority than the system has.
objectives: Distinguish a model response, deterministic workflow, bounded agent, and multi-agent work system.
Specify a task using goal, performance measure, environment, observations, allowed actions, state, and stop conditions.
Compare predictable, uncertain, observable, partially observable, static, and changing environments.
Identify language and interface choices that cause people to overstate agency, understanding, or authority.
Create a utility agent environment and authority specification.
subtopics: Rational-agent framing and its limits
Goals, performance measures, and goal complexity
Environment types and uncertainty
Observations, allowed actions, state, and tools
Reactivity, autonomy, and perceived agency
Human authority, prohibited action, and stop
expansions.workProduct: utility agent environment and authority specification
expansions.evidenceBoundary: The academic agent model is a design lens. It does not grant an artificial intelligence system legal, professional, or operating authority.

expansions.title: Planning, Reason and Act, reflection, and agentic retrieval
expansions.description: Compare fixed workflows with planning patterns that alternate reasoning, tool use, observation, evaluation, revision, and stop. Make observable evidence and control more important than hidden reasoning text.
objectives: Compare fixed workflow, plan-and-execute, Reason and Act, reflection, and agentic retrieval patterns.
Trace the observable goal, plan, action, tool result, evidence, evaluation, adjustment, and stop for one task.
Choose the least complicated planning pattern that can satisfy the utility task and consequence boundary.
Identify endless-loop, tool-selection, stale-evidence, plan-drift, and false-completion failures.
Create and test a governed agent plan and trace.
subtopics: Classical plan, language-model plan, and fixed workflow
Plan-and-execute
Reason and Act
Reflection and critique
Agentic retrieval and iterative source refinement
Evaluation, retry budget, escalation, and stop
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Do not expose private hidden reasoning or treat a generated reasoning narrative as proof. Evaluate observable actions, sources, tool results, and outcomes.

expansions.title: Multi-agent coordination, conflict, cost, and failure
expansions.description: Teach multiple agents as a coordinated work system with explicit roles, communication, shared state, arbitration, evidence, cost, and accountable human decision. More agents can create more failure as easily as more capability.
objectives: Choose among one workflow, one agent, and multiple specialist agents for a bounded utility task.
Design roles, messages, shared state, source versions, handoffs, arbitration, escalation, and final human authority.
Identify duplication, disagreement, stale state, deadlock, cascading error, excessive cost, and false consensus.
Use basic cooperation, incentive, and conflict reasoning without implying that agents are independent professionals.
Create and test a multi-agent coordination and recovery contract.
subtopics: Coordination topologies and orchestrators
Communication contracts and message evidence
Shared state, source versions, and conflict
Delegation, arbitration, consensus, and dissent
Deadlock, cascading failure, duplicated work, and cost multiplication
Human command, incident response, and final decision
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Multiple agents do not create independent truth, professional judgment, or legal authority. Preserve source versions, permissions, cost limits, dissent, and human decision rights.

expansions.title: Human-agent interaction and agentic user experience
expansions.description: Design the interaction that lets a person understand what the system is doing, inspect its evidence and limits, control consequential actions, interrupt work, correct mistakes, recover, and escalate.
objectives: Explain calibrated trust and common ground in plain English.
Distinguish transparency, explanation, source evidence, system status, confirmation, and human authority.
Design progress, preview, confirmation, cancel, interrupt, correction, recovery, and escalation behavior for a utility task.
Evaluate an interface for automation bias, false confidence, inaccessible interaction, hidden state, and weak failure recovery.
Create an agent interaction, authority, and recovery specification.
subtopics: Calibrated trust and common ground
Visible goal, plan, source, tool, status, limitation, and cost
Preview and confirmation before consequential action
Interrupt, cancel, pause, correct, undo, and recover
Confidence, uncertainty, explanation, and source display
Accessibility, plain language, escalation, and human handoff
expansions.workProduct: agent interaction, authority, and recovery specification
expansions.evidenceBoundary: A friendly or transparent interface does not make an answer accurate or an action authorized. Interface design must expose, not hide, the remaining evidence and authority limits.

expansions.title: Agent-specific evaluation and continuous assurance
expansions.description: Extend evaluation from answer quality to the complete agent trajectory, including task result, tool use, source coverage, policy behavior, recovery, latency, cost, and human-review effort.
objectives: Define task success and failure before selecting an agent metric.
Evaluate answer quality, groundedness, source coverage, tool-call correctness, trajectory, refusal, recovery, latency, cost, and human effort.
Build a representative test set with ordinary, boundary, adversarial, stale, conflicting, and failure cases.
Set acceptance thresholds, stop rules, regression tests, reviewers, and correction actions.
Create an agent evaluation and continuing-assurance plan.
subtopics: Task outcome and acceptance evidence
Groundedness, source coverage, and citation support
Tool-call correctness and trajectory evaluation
Policy, refusal, permission, and escalation behavior
Latency, cost, human effort, resilience, and recovery
Regression set, thresholds, drift, incident, and continuing assurance
expansions.evidenceBoundary: An average score or one successful demonstration does not prove fitness for a utility task, safety, fairness, compliance, or performance under changed conditions.

expansions.title: Observability, drift, degradation, and incident response
expansions.description: Teach how a team notices that data, sources, model behavior, prompts, tools, permissions, infrastructure, cost, or human work has changed, then pauses, investigates, corrects, and records the response.
objectives: Explain observability as the evidence needed to understand a changing system, not as a dashboard alone.
Distinguish data drift, concept drift, model degradation, retrieval staleness, prompt regression, tool failure, permission change, and workflow change.
Select signals, logs, traces, thresholds, alerts, owners, and response times for one utility application.
Investigate an incident without overwriting prior evidence and decide whether to continue, restrict, roll back, or stop.
Create an artificial intelligence observability and incident-response record.
subtopics: Signals, logs, traces, measures, alerts, and ownership
Data drift, concept drift, and model degradation
Retrieval staleness, source conflict, and prompt regression
Tool, permission, integration, infrastructure, and cost failure
Containment, pause, rollback, correction, and communication
Append-only incident, decision, and learning record
expansions.evidenceBoundary: A missing alert does not prove a system is healthy. Monitoring scope, blind spots, retention, privacy, and responsible human response must remain visible.

expansions.title: Release discipline for AI-assisted software building
expansions.description: Turn AI-assisted code generation into a controlled engineering process with plans, branches, reviews, tests, environments, dependencies, secrets, artifacts, release evidence, and recovery.
objectives: Explain repository, branch, change, review, test, commit, artifact, release, deployment, and rollback in plain English.
Set the files, systems, credentials, and actions an AI coding agent may inspect or change.
Review a change by reading the plan, difference, tests, security effect, and rollback path.
Reproduce a build in a clean environment without using an unrecorded local dependency or secret.
Create an AI-assisted software release evidence package.
subtopics: Goal, plan, issue, user story, and acceptance evidence
Repository, branch, difference, review, commit, and tag
Unit, integration, security, accessibility, and regression tests
Dependencies, lock files, environments, configuration, and secrets
Build artifact, release notes, approval, deployment, and rollback
AI coding-agent permissions, evidence, and human ownership
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Generated code and passing tests do not transfer engineering, cybersecurity, accessibility, privacy, or release responsibility to the artificial intelligence system.

expansions.title: Cloud foundations and managed AI platforms
expansions.description: Teach a vendor-neutral cloud foundation before a learner enters an Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, or other platform lab. Every managed service still has identity, data, logging, cost, support, and exit responsibilities.
objectives: Explain cloud region, network, compute, storage, identity, secret, log, managed model endpoint, and service responsibility in plain English.
Map data and request flow across a minimum supportable hosted artificial intelligence application.
Compare managed, self-hosted, local, and hybrid patterns for capability, control, privacy, cost, support, and exit.
Identify identity, permission, secret, network, logging, backup, cost, resilience, and vendor-dependency requirements.
Create a vendor-neutral cloud AI responsibility and exit map.
subtopics: Regions, networks, compute, storage, and managed services
Identity, role, permission, secret, and key rotation
Managed model and agent platforms
Logs, backups, resilience, rate, capacity, and recovery
Consumption cost, budgets, alerts, and support ownership
Portability, data export, contract, lock-in, and exit
expansions.workProduct: cloud AI responsibility and exit map
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Named platforms are dated examples. A managed service does not remove the utility's responsibility for data, access, evaluation, contract, cost, records, or accountable use.

expansions.title: Synthetic media, deepfakes, disinformation, and content integrity
expansions.description: Prepare learners to verify generated and altered media, preserve source and transformation records, disclose synthetic content, control publication, respond to false public information, and correct the record.
objectives: Distinguish generated media, edited media, misleading context, impersonation, deepfake, error, satire, and deliberate disinformation.
Inspect source, author, capture time, transformation, metadata, corroboration, approval, and publication history.
Design disclosure, approval, accessibility, retention, correction, and incident rules for utility communication.
Respond to a false water-quality, service, emergency, or public-official message without amplifying unsupported content.
Create a utility synthetic-media integrity and correction protocol.
subtopics: Generated, edited, synthetic, misleading, and impersonated media
Source, metadata, provenance, transformation, and corroboration
Employee, vendor, public-official, and community communication risks
Disclosure, consent, accessibility, approval, and publication
Detection limits, evidence preservation, and escalation
Public correction, incident communication, and trust repair
expansions.workProduct: utility synthetic-media integrity and correction protocol
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Detection tools are imperfect. Do not label media authentic or false without recorded evidence, qualified review, and an honest statement of uncertainty.

expansions.title: Explainability, transparency, trace, and justification
expansions.description: Teach the difference among an understandable explanation, a source trace, an interpretable model, a decision justification, and an unknown mechanism. Match the evidence burden to the consequence and audience.
objectives: Distinguish explanation, transparency, interpretability, traceability, provenance, evidence, and decision justification.
Identify what a model, application, vendor, reviewer, and accountable decision maker can and cannot explain.
Match explanation and evidence needs to the task, consequence, affected person, professional standard, and decision right.
Reject an explanation that is fluent but unsupported, incomplete, inapplicable, or disconnected from the actual system record.
Create an explanation, evidence, and decision-justification record.
subtopics: Plain-language explanation and audience
Model interpretability and technical limits
Application transparency and system status
Traceability, provenance, source evidence, and version
Decision justification, accountable owner, and affected person
Unknowns, uncertainty, challenge, correction, and appeal
expansions.evidenceBoundary: A plausible explanation can be wrong. Provenance can show origin without proving accuracy. Human justification remains separate from model output.

expansions.title: Adoption methods, psychological safety, champions, and operating models
expansions.description: Turn adoption into a designed operating change involving tasks, identity, participation, learning, support, feedback, labor boundaries, champion networks, and clear decision rights.
objectives: Explain why software launch, training attendance, compliance, confidence, and responsible adoption are different outcomes.
Compare structured change methods and select only the parts that fit the utility situation.
Design participation, psychological safety, champion, training, support, feedback, correction, and escalation mechanisms.
Compare centralized, federated, and hybrid artificial intelligence operating models and centers of excellence.
Create a workforce adoption, participation, and support plan.
subtopics: Task, identity, confidence, concern, participation, and professional authority
Kotter, ADKAR, McKinsey 7S, and fit-to-purpose use
Psychological safety, challenge, reporting, and correction
Champions, peer learning, office hours, and support
Centralized, federated, hybrid, and center-of-excellence models
Labor, privacy, accessibility, incentives, feedback, and measurement
expansions.workProduct: workforce adoption, participation, and support plan
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Do not label concern as resistance, use learning records as hidden job-performance evidence, or promise adoption from communication and training alone.

expansions.title: Value measurement and benefit realization
expansions.description: Create one measurement spine from the current baseline through adoption, quality, risk, cost, review effort, time to value, benefit ownership, measurement cadence, and the decision to continue or stop.
objectives: Distinguish output, activity, adoption, quality, service outcome, risk reduction, financial value, and public value.
Define a credible current baseline before estimating a benefit.
Build measures for quality, error, delay, rework, human review, cost, risk, adoption, and affected service outcomes.
Assign a benefit owner, source, frequency, threshold, limitation, review, and stop rule for every material measure.
Create a utility AI value and benefit-realization record.
subtopics: Problem, current process, baseline, and counterfactual
Activity, adoption, quality, risk, service, financial, and public-value measures
Direct, indirect, shifted, avoided, and uncertain cost
Human-review effort, correction, and operating burden
Benefit owner, data source, cadence, threshold, and limitation
Continue, redesign, defer, scale, or stop decision
expansions.workProduct: utility AI value and benefit-realization record
expansions.evidenceBoundary: Do not promise productivity, savings, return, staff reduction, service improvement, or public value without an approved baseline, complete cost, measured evidence, and accountable owner.
